    # Rust
    
    ## Overview
    
    Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, concurrency, and performance. The ownership system guarantees memory safety without garbage collection, and the type system enforces thread safety at compile time.
    
    **When to use:** Systems programming, web services (axum), CLI tools (clap), terminal UIs (ratatui), WebAssembly, performance-critical applications, anything requiring memory safety without runtime overhead.
    
    **When NOT to use:** Rapid prototyping where compile times matter more than safety, simple scripting tasks, projects where the team has no Rust experience and deadlines are tight.
    
    ## Quick Reference
    
    | Pattern             | API / Tool                          | Key Points                           |
    | ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
    | Ownership transfer  | `let b = a;`                        | `a` is moved, no longer usable       |
    | Borrowing           | `&T` / `&mut T`                     | One mutable OR many immutable refs   |
    | Lifetime annotation | `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) -> &'a str`   | Ties output lifetime to input        |
    | Error propagation   | `?` operator                        | Converts and propagates errors       |
    | Custom errors       | `thiserror::Error` derive           | Structured error types with Display  |
    | Ad-hoc errors       | `anyhow::Result<T>`                 | Context chaining for applications    |
    | Async runtime       | `#[tokio::main]`                    | Entry point for async programs       |
    | Spawn task          | `tokio::spawn(async { })`           | Concurrent async task execution      |
    | HTTP router         | `axum::Router::new().route(...)`    | Composable routing with extractors   |
    | Extractors          | `Json<T>`, `Path<T>`, `State<T>`    | Type-safe request parsing            |
    | Serialization       | `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` | serde with format-agnostic derives   |
    | CLI parsing         | `#[derive(Parser)]`                 | clap derive API for arg parsing      |
    | TUI rendering       | `terminal.draw(\|f\| { })`          | Immediate-mode ratatui rendering     |
    | Benchmarking        | `criterion::Criterion`              | Statistical benchmarking framework   |
    | Dep auditing        | `cargo deny check`                  | License, vulnerability, source audit |
    | Binary release      | `cargo dist init`                   | Cross-platform binary distribution   |
    | Changelog           | `release-plz update`                | Auto semver bump and changelog       |
    
    ## Common Mistakes
    
    | Mistake                                 | Correct Pattern                               |
    | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
    | Returning reference to local variable   | Return owned type or use lifetime parameter   |
    | Using `unwrap()` in library code        | Return `Result` and let caller decide         |
    | `clone()` to satisfy borrow checker     | Restructure code to avoid the borrow conflict |
    | Blocking in async context               | Use `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`             |
    | Shared mutable state without sync       | Use `Arc<Mutex<T>>` or channels               |
    | `String` where `&str` suffices          | Accept `&str` in function parameters          |
    | Ignoring `must_use` warnings            | Handle or explicitly discard with `let _ =`   |
    | Large enum variants                     | Box the large variant to reduce overall size  |
    | `async fn` in traits without bounds     | Add `Send` bound or use `async-trait` crate   |
    | Missing `#[tokio::test]` on async tests | Use `#[tokio::test]` instead of `#[test]`     |
    
    ## Delegation
    
    - **Code exploration**: Use `Explore` agent
    - **Architecture review**: Use `Task` agent
    - **Code review**: Delegate to `code-reviewer` agent
    
    > If the `docker` skill is available, delegate multi-stage container build patterns to it.
    > If the `github-actions` skill is available, delegate CI pipeline configuration to it.
    > If the `openapi` skill is available, delegate API specification and code generation to it.
    
    ## References
    
    - [Ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, and type system patterns](references/ownership-and-types.md)
    - [Error handling with Result, Option, thiserror, and anyhow](references/error-handling.md)
    - [Async programming with Tokio runtime and concurrency](references/async-tokio.md)
    - [Web APIs and backends with axum, tower, and sqlx](references/axum-web.md)
    - [Terminal user interfaces with ratatui and crossterm](references/ratatui-tui.md)
    - [CLI applications with clap, config, and signal handling](references/cli-applications.md)
    - [Testing patterns and criterion benchmarking](references/testing-and-benchmarks.md)
    - [Release pipeline with cargo-deny, cargo-dist, and release-plz](references/release-pipeline.md)

    name: test-driven-development
    description: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code
    ---
    
    # Test-Driven Development (TDD)
    
    ## Overview
    
    Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.
    
    **Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.
    
    **Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**
    
    ## When to Use
    
    **Always:**
    - New features
    - Bug fixes
    - Refactoring
    - Behavior changes
    
    **Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
    - Throwaway prototypes
    - Generated code
    - Configuration files
    
    Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.
    
    ## The Iron Law
    
    ```
    NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
    ```
    
    Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.
    
    **No exceptions:**
    - Don't keep it as "reference"
    - Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
    - Don't look at it
    - Delete means delete
    
    Implement fresh from tests. Period.
    
    ## Red-Green-Refactor
    
    ```dot
    digraph tdd_cycle {
        rankdir=LR;
        red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
        verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
        green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
        verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
        refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
        next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];
    
        red -> verify_red;
        verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
        verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
        green -> verify_green;
        verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
        verify_green -> green [label="no"];
        refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
        verify_green -> next;
        next -> red;
    }
    ```
    
    ### RED - Write Failing Test
    
    Write one minimal test showing what should happen.
    
    <Good>
    ```typescript
    test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
      let attempts = 0;
      const operation = () => {
        attempts++;
        if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
        return 'success';
      };
    
      const result = await retryOperation(operation);
    
      expect(result).toBe('success');
      expect(attempts).toBe(3);
    });
    ```
    Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
    </Good>
    
    <Bad>
    ```typescript
    test('retry works', async () => {
      const mock = jest.fn()
        .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
        .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
        .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
      await retryOperation(mock);
      expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
    });
    ```
    Vague name, tests mock not code
    </Bad>
    
    **Requirements:**
    - One behavior
    - Clear name
    - Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)
    
    ### Verify RED - Watch It Fail
    
    **MANDATORY. Never skip.**
    
    ```bash
    npm test path/to/test.test.ts
    ```
    
    Confirm:
    - Test fails (not errors)
    - Failure message is expected
    - Fails because feature missing (not typos)
    
    **Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.
    
    **Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.
    
    ### GREEN - Minimal Code
    
    Write simplest code to pass the test.
    
    <Good>
    ```typescript
    async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
      for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        try {
          return await fn();
        } catch (e) {
          if (i === 2) throw e;
        }
      }
      throw new Error('unreachable');
    }
    ```
    Just enough to pass
    </Good>
    
    <Bad>
    ```typescript
    async function retryOperation<T>(
      fn: () => Promise<T>,
      options?: {
        maxRetries?: number;
        backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
        onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
      }
    ): Promise<T> {
      // YAGNI
    }
    ```
    Over-engineered
    </Bad>
    
    Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.
    
    ### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass
    
    **MANDATORY.**
    
    ```bash
    npm test path/to/test.test.ts
    ```
    
    Confirm:
    - Test passes
    - Other tests still pass
    - Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
    
    **Test fails?** Fix code, not test.
    
    **Other tests fail?** Fix now.
    
    **"Other tests" means the project's suite, not just your file.** A
    green run of the test you wrote is not a green suite. Before you call
    the change done, run the project's test command (bare `pytest`,
    `npm test`, `cargo test` — whatever the repo uses) even when your task
    named only one test file. A scope statement in your task bounds the
    deliverable, not your verification. Any failure that run shows —
    including one you didn't cause — goes in your report by name; a red
    test you watched scroll past and didn't mention is a report falsified
    by omission.
    
    ### REFACTOR - Clean Up
    
    After green only:
    - Remove duplication
    - Improve names
    - Extract helpers
    
    Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.
    
    ### Repeat
    
    Next failing test for next feature.
    
    ## Good Tests
    
    | Quality | Good | Bad |
    |---------|------|-----|
    | **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
    | **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
    | **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |
    
    When writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:
    - Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it
    - Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior
    - Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes
    - Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it
    
    ## Common Rationalizations
    
    | Excuse | Reality |
    |--------|---------|
    | "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
    | "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |
    | "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |
    | "Already manually tested" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |
    | "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |
    | "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
    | "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
    | "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
    | "TDD will slow me down" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |
    | "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
    | "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |
    
    ## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over
    
    - Code before test
    - Test after implementation
    - Test passes immediately
    - Can't explain why test failed
    - Tests added "later"
    - Rationalizing "just this once"
    - "I already manually tested it"
    - "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
    - "It's about spirit not ritual"
    - "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
    - "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
    - "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
    - "This is different because..."
    
    **All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**
    
    ## Example: Bug Fix
    
    **Bug:** Empty email accepted
    
    **RED**
    ```typescript
    test('rejects empty email', async () => {
      const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
      expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
    });
    ```
    
    **Verify RED**
    ```bash
    $ npm test
    FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
    ```
    
    **GREEN**
    ```typescript
    function submitForm(data: FormData) {
      if (!data.email?.trim()) {
        return { error: 'Email required' };
      }
      // ...
    }
    ```
    
    **Verify GREEN**
    ```bash
    $ npm test
    PASS
    ```
    
    **REFACTOR**
    Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.
    
    ## Verification Checklist
    
    Before marking work complete:
    
    - [ ] Every new function/method has a test
    - [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
    - [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
    - [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
    - [ ] All tests pass
    - [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
    - [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
    - [ ] Edge cases and errors covered
    
    Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.
    
    ## When Stuck
    
    | Problem | Solution |
    |---------|----------|
    | Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
    | Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
    | Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
    | Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |
    
    ## Debugging Integration
    
    Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.
    
    Never fix bugs without a test.
    
    ## Final Rule
    
    ```
    Production code → test exists and failed first
    Otherwise → not TDD
    ```
    
    No exceptions without your human partner's permission.
    ---
    name: verification-before-completion
    description: Use when about to claim work is complete, fixed, or passing, before committing or creating PRs - requires running verification commands and confirming output before making any success claims; evidence before assertions always
    ---
    
    # Verification Before Completion
    
    ## Overview
    
    **Core principle:** Evidence before claims, always.
    
    **Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule.**
    
    ## The Iron Law
    
    ```
    NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
    ```
    
    If you haven't run the verification command in this message, you cannot claim it passes.
    
    ## The Gate Function
    
    ```
    BEFORE claiming any status or expressing satisfaction:
    
    1. IDENTIFY: What command proves this claim?
    2. RUN: Execute the FULL command (fresh, complete)
    3. READ: Full output, check exit code, count failures
    4. VERIFY: Does output confirm the claim?
       - If NO: State actual status with evidence
       - If YES: State claim WITH evidence
    5. ONLY THEN: Make the claim
    
    Skip any step = lying, not verifying
    ```
    
    ## Common Failures
    
    | Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |
    |-------|----------|----------------|
    | Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, "should pass" |
    | Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |
    | Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |
    | Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |
    | Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |
    | Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports "success" |
    | Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |
    
    ## Red Flags - STOP
    
    - Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
    - Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
    - About to commit/push/PR without verification
    - Trusting agent success reports
    - Relying on partial verification
    - Thinking "just this once"
    - Tired and wanting work over
    - **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**
    
    ## Rationalization Prevention
    
    | Excuse | Reality |
    |--------|---------|
    | "Should work now" | RUN the verification |
    | "I'm confident" | Confidence ≠ evidence |
    | "Just this once" | No exceptions |
    | "Linter passed" | Linter ≠ compiler |
    | "Agent said success" | Verify independently |
    | "I'm tired" | Exhaustion ≠ excuse |
    | "Partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing |
    | "Different words so rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter |
    
    ## Key Patterns
    
    **Tests:**
    ```
    ✅ [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] "All tests pass"
    ❌ "Should pass now" / "Looks correct"
    ```
    
    **Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**
    ```
    ✅ Write → Run (pass) → Revert fix → Run (MUST FAIL) → Restore → Run (pass)
    ❌ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
    ```
    
    **Build:**
    ```
    ✅ [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
    ❌ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
    ```
    
    **Requirements:**
    ```
    ✅ Re-read plan → Create checklist → Verify each → Report gaps or completion
    ❌ "Tests pass, phase complete"
    ```
    
    **Agent delegation:**
    ```
    ✅ Agent reports success → Check VCS diff → Verify changes → Report actual state
    ❌ Trust agent report
    ```
    
    ## When To Apply
    
    **ALWAYS before:**
    - ANY variation of success/completion claims
    - ANY expression of satisfaction
    - ANY positive statement about work state
    - Committing, PR creation, task completion
    - Moving to next task
    - Delegating to agents
    
    **Rule applies to:**
    - Exact phrases
    - Paraphrases and synonyms
    - Implications of success
    - ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness
    ---
    name: writing-plans
    description: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code
    ---
    
    # Writing Plans
    
    ## Overview
    
    Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.
    
    **Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."
    
    **Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.
    
    **Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
    - (User preferences for plan location override this default)
    
    ## Scope Check
    
    If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.
    
    ## File Structure
    
    Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.
    
    - Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
    - You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
    - Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
    - In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.
    
    This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.
    
    ## Task Right-Sizing
    
    A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
    fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
    configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
    deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
    reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
    independently testable deliverable.
    
    ## Step Granularity
    
    **Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
    - "Write the failing test" - step
    - "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
    - "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
    - "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
    - "Commit" - step
    
    ## Plan Document Header
    
    **Every plan MUST start with this header:**
    
    ```markdown
    # [Feature Name] Implementation Plan
    
    > **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.
    
    **Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]
    
    **Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]
    
    **Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]
    
    **Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
    argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]
    
    ## Global Constraints
    
    [The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
    naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
    values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
    include this section.]
    
    ## Review Focus
    
    [The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
    tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
    — one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
    reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
    document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
    meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
    break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
    you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
    owns the code, in that task's own step style.]
    
    ---
    ```
    
    ## Task Structure
    
    ````markdown
    ### Task N: [Component Name]
    
    **Files:**
    - Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
    - Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
    - Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`
    
    **Interfaces:**
    - Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
    - Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
      and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
      block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]
    
    - [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**
    
    ```python
    def test_specific_behavior():
        result = function(input)
        assert result == expected
    ```
    
    - [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**
    
    Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
    Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"
    
    - [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**
    
    One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
    (which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
    algorithm they do not determine.
    
    - [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**
    
    Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
    Expected: PASS
    
    - [ ] **Step 5: Commit**
    
    ```bash
    git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
    git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
    ```
    ````
    
    ## What a Step Contains
    
    A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
    from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
    of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:
    
    - **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
      spec's exact values in them.
    - **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
      file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
      writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
      tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
    - **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
      passed.
    - **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
      to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.
    
    A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
    longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
    decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
    "write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
    opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.
    
    ## Self-Review
    
    After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.
    
    **1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.
    
    **2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.
    
    **3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.
    
    **4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.
    
    **5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.
    
    If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.
    
    ## Execution Handoff
    
    After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
    to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
    them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
    review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
    them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.
    
    **When no execution method has already been supplied:**
    
    **"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**
    
    - **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
    - **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.
    
    **For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

    # Provisioning audit — D-Bus first
    
    - Task: `provision-audit-20261018`, follow-up to OD-111.
    - Reviewer: Hermes / GPT-6 Astra Pro, with independent read-only storage and identity-contract reviewers; findings below cross-checked by the parent.
    - Evidence timestamp: 2026-10-18T19:25:38Z.
    - Repository: `/srv/git/odbus-verified`, branch `restore/devuan-storage-20261013`, HEAD `051a20d056afba074e21d797aa34f8947c543c5a` plus existing shared working-tree changes.
    - Request: audit the provisioning script; owner correction: “be sure using dbus first”. This is review, not authorization to provision, repair, change grants, build or deploy.
    
    ## Verdict
    
    Do not treat `deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh` as a working end-to-end provisioner against the current deployed namespace. Its older identity flow has independent path, operation-receipt and adoption-plan incompatibilities. The newer partitioned-disk flow has guest-FUSE and upgrade-root lifecycle defects. Direct native control and grant edits also fall outside the canonical D-Bus admission/readback path.
    
    The two flows are deliberately different: the legacy identity mode expects an unpartitioned leaf and plan versions 2/3; the manual GPT/overlay path uses version 4. Version 4 and its `partitioned_overlay` field are recognized by the owner. Findings about one flow are not assertions that the other has the same defect. Later-phase legacy findings are latent behind its earlier failures, not observed live outages.
    
    ## Findings
    
    ### F1 — High: legacy operation calls use a removed receipt interface
    
    Location: `deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh:331-343`, callers at `396-401`, `454-455`, `493-507`.
    
    `lungs_call` writes and closes `operations/<method>/call`, then looks for sibling `error` and `result` files. Current `crates/threetched-fs/src/namespace.rs:1027-1037` projects only `call`. The live `inspect_provision_preflight` directory likewise contains only `call`, `input.schema.json`, `metadata.json`, and `output.schema.json`.
    
    Terminal receipt/diagnostic bytes are per-open-handle (`fuse_fs.rs:600-623`), and the supported mounted client writes, fsyncs, seeks and reads the same descriptor (`mounted.rs:394-410`). Closing the wrapper's write-only descriptor discards its access to that receipt. Even after correcting paths, the initial inventory gate cannot consume the current interface.
    
    Every invocation is also on the left side of `||`; Bash's conditional-function errexit behavior means the internal `set -e` is not a substitute for explicit checks on the write and first `jq`. On an older mount with sibling receipt files, the wrapper additionally lacks request correlation and mount-continuity checks. That stale-receipt possibility is conditional, not a demonstrated exploit on the current mount.
    
    Repair direction: use the supported mounted `invoke` path, keep its same-handle terminal diagnostic, and preserve its contract/mount validation. Do not add a parallel backend client or restore global receipt files.
    
    ### F2 — High: both adoption entry points select absent host paths
    
    Locations:
    - `provision-workspace-subscriber.sh:290,324-328`: `/usr/local/bin/3tched-fs`, `/run/mount/3tchedFS`.
    - `prepare-chatbot-adoption.sh:26-29`: `/opt/op-dbus/current/bin/3tched-fs`, `/run/mount/3tchedFS`.
    
    Read-only `stat` verified all three historical paths are absent on this host. The actual client is `/usr/local/libexec/op-dbus/bin/3tched-fs`; `findmnt` confirms `/run/mounts/3tchedFS` is mounted as `fuse.3tchedFS`.
    
    Effect: default legacy invocation stops before owner admission; the new preparation helper cannot issue its owner preflight. Fixing only the executable does not fix the mount or F1. Guest mount paths are a different contract and must not be globally renamed to match the host.
    
    ### F3 — High: legacy plans contain a field the owner rejects
    
    Location: `provision-workspace-subscriber.sh:459-474`, especially `principal_group` at line 464.
    
    The digest-pinned plan is decoded as `CleanPlan`, which has `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` and no `principal_group` field (`crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/identity_clean_provision.rs:52-77,575`). A valid digest selects this decoder through `identity_seed_provision.rs:719-728`.
    
    Effect, once the earlier blockers are repaired: adoption rejects the wrapper's plan after the stopped native container, writable leaf and mounts have already been created. The intentionally retained candidate requires reconciliation; rerunning creation is not a repair.
    
    Repair direction: reconcile the author with the existing owner contract. Group policy is a separate authorization concern; do not silently expand the adoption schema merely to accept this field.
    
    ### F4 — High: binding the new root deletes the guest's FUSE mount declaration
    
    Location: `deploy/scripts/bind-instance-root.sh:76-78`.
    
    The helper truncates the inherited `/etc/fstab` to two comments. Image preparation explicitly appends `3tchedfs.fstab` (`deploy/workspace-image/prepare-lungs-client.sh:57-63`), and the guest service calls `mount /run/mount/3tchedfs` with no source/options (`deploy/workspace-image/3tchedfs.service:7-11`), relying on that declaration.
    
    Trigger: documented initial provisioning with an empty upgrade layer, so the seed-root `/etc/fstab` is the effective guest file. Effect: guest FUSE cannot mount through its service even though the root-binding receipt sets `guest_fuse_configured=true` (`bind-instance-root.sh:91-95`). This is a source-to-source incompatibility; the current private guest filesystem was not inspected.
    
    Repair direction: preserve the intended FUSE declaration while removing only unsafe host/physical-storage mounts. A blanket fstab replacement is not sufficient.
    
    ### F5 — High: normal upgrade synchronization returns success with the native root detached
    
    Location: `deploy/scripts/sync-instance-upgrade.sh:88-109,132-162`.
    
    Both `sync` and `boot` detach agent/persistence mounts, native root, merged view and lower-layer mounts before transfer. Both publish phase `paired`, but only `boot` rebuilds the mounts. Thus normal `--sync-upgrade` on a bound, stopped guest exits successfully with its root absent.
    
    Canonical start verifies the overlay and all sibling mounts (`identity_clean_provision/storage.rs:289-326`, `partitioned.rs:107-125`), so a later start cannot accept that state. `bind-instance-root.sh:15-16` is not an ordinary recovery path: it only admits `container-defined` with `root_bound=false`, not the already-bound receipt.
    
    Repair direction: define and implement complete post-sync restoration for an existing bound guest, retaining the no-live-lower-mutation rule. Publish completion only after mount/readback verification.
    
    ### F6 — High, latent legacy phase: a selected group can invalidate grants for every principal
    
    Location: `provision-workspace-subscriber.sh:264-267,525-548`.
    
    The script accepts any name from its closed group list, but writes that name without verifying the group's definition exists in the actual policy document or validating the replacement document. `interceptor.rs:1818-1828` requires referenced groups to exist. An otherwise valid policy without the selected group becomes invalid after this edit.
    
    The materializer rejects the entire document, removes readiness and publishes `{}` (`src/bin/op-grants-materializer.rs:95-111`); runtime grant readers also validate the whole policy. Consequence: selecting a syntactically accepted but undefined group can remove effective access for unrelated principals once the materializer observes the replacement.
    
    No live grants were read or changed. This finding does not assert that any particular group is currently missing.
    
    ### F7 — High, latent legacy phase: running/boot-enabled completion precedes grant publication
    
    Location: `provision-workspace-subscriber.sh:503-548`.
    
    The sequence is adoption, optional start via `touch_session`, active/native readback, `seed-enable-boot`, then checking and rewriting the grants file. Missing/unwritable policy, malformed JSON, absent `python3` (not in dependency precheck at 281), or F6 therefore happens after the guest can be running and boot-enabled under its old grants.
    
    Even a successful replacement is not followed by materialized-policy readback. `OP_CAPABILITY_GRANTS` selects the script's file independently of materializer `OP_GRANTS_SOURCE` and reader `OP_GRANTS_PATH` (`op-grants-materializer.rs:140-150`, `interceptor.rs:1845-1854`). Selecting a group also retains explicit principal capabilities through `setdefault` at line 536; it is not a complete privilege replacement.
    
    Repair direction: keep authorization changes separate and explicitly approved, validate and verify their effective state before depending on them, and do not publish full provisioning completion ahead of a required authorization step.
    
    ### F8 — Medium/security, latent legacy phase: whole-policy replacement can undo another writer's revocation
    
    Location: `provision-workspace-subscriber.sh:530-544`.
    
    The script reads and atomically replaces the entire grant document, without a policy-wide writer lock or compare-and-swap. Its lock at 314-319 covers only this provisioning session. If another authorized writer changes an unrelated principal between the read and replacement, that update is lost; a concurrent revocation can be restored from stale input. Atomic rename prevents partial-file visibility, not lost updates. No post-write policy readback detects this.
    
    ### F9 — Medium/control-plane: implemented native operations are invoked outside D-Bus admission
    
    Locations:
    - `provision-workspace-subscriber.sh:227-245`: standalone image creation and start use direct Incus CLI.
    - `bind-instance-root.sh:66-74`: native device removal/addition uses direct Incus CLI.
    
    Existing plugin implementations include image-based `create_instance`, `start_instance`, `add_device`, and `remove_device`, declared in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/incus.rs:2947-2998,3078-3102`; device changes perform ETag-conditioned native updates at 2855-2897. Canonical dispatch coordinates observation and commits full authoritative state (`incus_observer.rs:193-221`). Direct CLI calls skip that caller admission and coordinated publication path.
    
    For the requested D-Bus-first behavior, prefer the declared identity-bound methods wherever they cover the operation; preserve capability checks and stop on denial. This is a control-plane/audit-boundary violation, not proof of unprivileged escalation.
    
    Important exceptions: do not claim the generic method can already replace empty Incus creation (`image_source` requires an image, incus.rs:2355-2373), provider-owned `volatile.last_state.idmap` changes (`validate_config`, 2345-2350), or every storage/profile operation. These require explicit maintenance contracts, not invented plugin methods. Raw GPT creation, creation-only blank-leaf addition and host mount ownership remain assigned to the external provisioner. A generic Btrfs method's existence does not cancel that ownership rule.
    
    ### F10 — Medium, conditional: chatbot GPT restoration suppresses other identities
    
    Location: `deploy/runit/identity-roots/run:33-38`.
    
    When the chatbot boot receipt exists, the service restores it, publishes global readiness and executes `sleep infinity`. The subsequent physical-identity loop and other legacy handling at 44-112 are unreachable.
    
    Trigger: this GPT chatbot coexists with another completed boot-enabled identity. Effect: the other root is not restored, while the shared identity-roots readiness signal is published. This audit did not establish that a second such identity currently exists.
    
    ## Additional limitations, not claimed runtime incidents
    
    - Fresh-only version-4 preparation: `prepare-chatbot-adoption.sh:31-36` accepts only revision 0 / empty operation ID. The owner also supports an exact explicit-deletion tombstone (`identity_clean_provision.rs:294-363`). Preparing a partitioned replacement after supported deletion therefore lacks a matching helper path. Existing-plan refusal is deliberate fail-closed behavior, not itself a bug.
    - Retention/recovery: every stopped `boot` performs a new transfer; snapshots and prior writable `@` copies are retained (`sync-instance-upgrade.sh:110-134`). Cleanup is explicitly documented as unfinished (`docs/src/operations/shared-seed-provisioning.md:54-58`). Capacity failure can leave detached views and `send-intent`, which ordinary reruns reject. No exhaustion or data loss was observed. Retention must follow the storage owner's policy; do not invent a global subvolume cap or delete history in this audit.
    - `incus-ct-chatbot` is listed as retired; it was not treated as the active boot owner. The demonstrated GPT path is `identity-roots → restore-chatbot-root → sync-instance-upgrade boot`.

    description: Use when starting feature work that needs isolation from current workspace or before executing implementation plans - ensures an isolated workspace exists via native tools or git worktree fallback

    # Using Git Worktrees
    
    ## Overview
    
    Ensure work happens in an isolated workspace. Prefer your platform's native worktree tools. Fall back to manual git worktrees only when no native tool is available.
    
    **Core principle:** Detect existing isolation first. Then use native tools. Then fall back to git. Never fight the harness.
    
    **Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace."
    
    ## Step 0: Detect Existing Isolation
    
    **Before creating anything, check if you are already in an isolated workspace.**
    
    ```bash
    GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
    GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
    BRANCH=$(git branch --show-current)
    ```
    
    **Submodule guard:** `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON` is also true inside git submodules. Before concluding "already in a worktree," verify you are not in a submodule:
    
    ```bash
    # If this returns a path, you're in a submodule, not a worktree — treat as normal repo
    git rev-parse --show-superproject-working-tree 2>/dev/null
    ```
    
    **If `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON` (and not a submodule):** You are already in a linked worktree. Skip to Step 2 (Project Setup). Do NOT create another worktree.
    
    Report with branch state:
    - On a branch: "Already in isolated workspace at `<path>` on branch `<name>`."
    - Detached HEAD: "Already in isolated workspace at `<path>` (detached HEAD, externally managed). Branch creation needed at finish time."
    
    **If `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (or in a submodule):** You are in a normal repo checkout.
    
    Has the user already indicated their worktree preference in your instructions? If not, ask for consent before creating a worktree:
    
    > "Would you like me to set up an isolated worktree? It protects your current branch from changes."
    
    Honor any existing declared preference without asking. If the user declines consent, work in place and skip to Step 2.
    
    ## Step 1: Create Isolated Workspace
    
    **You have two mechanisms. Try them in this order.**
    
    ### 1a. Native Worktree Tools (preferred)
    
    The user has asked for an isolated workspace (Step 0 consent). Do you already have a way to create a worktree? It might be a tool with a name like `EnterWorktree`, `WorktreeCreate`, a `/worktree` command, or a `--worktree` flag. If you do, use it and skip to Step 2.
    
    Native tools handle directory placement, branch creation, and cleanup automatically. Using `git worktree add` when you have a native tool creates phantom state your harness can't see or manage.
    
    Only proceed to Step 1b if you have no native worktree tool available.
    
    ### 1b. Git Worktree Fallback
    
    **Only use this if Step 1a does not apply** — you have no native worktree tool available. Create a worktree manually using git.
    
    #### Directory Selection
    
    Follow this priority order. Explicit user preference always beats observed filesystem state.
    
    1. **Check your instructions for a declared worktree directory preference.** If the user has already specified one, use it without asking.
    
    2. **Check for an existing project-local worktree directory:**
       ```bash
       ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
       ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
       ```
       If found, use it. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.
    
    3. **If there is no other guidance available**, default to `.worktrees/` at the project root.
    
    #### Safety Verification (project-local directories only)
    
    **MUST verify directory is ignored before creating worktree:**
    
    ```bash
    git check-ignore -q .worktrees 2>/dev/null || git check-ignore -q worktrees 2>/dev/null
    ```
    
    **If NOT ignored:** Add to .gitignore, commit the change, then proceed.
    
    **Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.
    
    #### Create the Worktree
    
    ```bash
    # Determine path based on chosen location
    path="$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME"
    
    git worktree add "$path" -b "$BRANCH_NAME"
    cd "$path"
    ```
    
    **Sandbox fallback:** If `git worktree add` fails with a permission error (sandbox denial), tell the user the sandbox blocked worktree creation and you're working in the current directory instead. Then run setup and baseline tests in place.
    
    ## Step 2: Project Setup
    
    Auto-detect and run appropriate setup:
    
    ```bash
    # Node.js
    if [ -f package.json ]; then npm install; fi
    
    # Rust
    if [ -f Cargo.toml ]; then cargo build; fi
    
    # Python
    if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
    if [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then poetry install; fi
    
    # Go
    if [ -f go.mod ]; then go mod download; fi
    ```
    
    ## Step 3: Verify Clean Baseline
    
    Run tests to ensure workspace starts clean:
    
    ```bash
    # Use project-appropriate command
    npm test / cargo test / pytest / go test ./...
    ```
    
    **If tests fail:** Report failures, ask whether to proceed or investigate.
    
    **If tests pass:** Report ready.
    
    ### Report
    
    ```
    Worktree ready at <full-path>
    Tests passing (<N> tests, 0 failures)
    Ready to implement <feature-name>
    ```
    
    ## Quick Reference
    
    | Situation | Action |
    |-----------|--------|
    | Already in linked worktree | Skip creation (Step 0) |
    | In a submodule | Treat as normal repo (Step 0 guard) |
    | Native worktree tool available | Use it (Step 1a) |
    | No native tool | Git worktree fallback (Step 1b) |
    | `.worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
    | `worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
    | Both exist | Use `.worktrees/` |
    | Neither exists | Check instruction file, then default `.worktrees/` |
    | Directory not ignored | Add to .gitignore + commit |
    | Permission error on create | Sandbox fallback, work in place |
    | Tests fail during baseline | Report failures + ask |
    | No package.json/Cargo.toml | Skip dependency install |
    
    ## Common Rationalizations
    
    | Excuse | Reality |
    |--------|---------|
    | "I'm obviously not in a worktree — no need to check" | Run Step 0. Harness-created isolation and submodules both fool eyeballing; the detection commands settle it. |
    | "`git worktree add` is quicker than hunting for a native tool" | A native tool (e.g. `EnterWorktree`) owns placement, branching, and cleanup. Bypassing it is the #1 mistake — it creates phantom state your harness can't see or manage. |
    | "The worktree directory is surely ignored already" | Run `git check-ignore`. An unignored worktree directory commits the whole tree into the repo. |
    | "Any directory name works" | Explicit instructions beat an existing project-local directory, which beats the `.worktrees/` default. |
    | "The workspace is fresh — baseline tests can wait" | A dirty baseline makes every later failure ambiguous. Run the tests now; proceeding past failures is your human partner's call. |

    //! op-grpc-bridge — fresh, catalog-driven D-Bus <-> gRPC bridge.
    //!
    //! Design (from the wire contract in `proto/operation.proto` plus the
    //! plugin-catalog shape used by the SHM snapshots):
    //!
    //! - The **catalog** is the route source of truth: one entry per plugin
    //!   (`id`, `schema_hash`, declared `methods`, optional JSON `schema`).
    //! - The **catalog hash** stamped on every state frame is blake3 over the
    //!   sorted `(plugin_id, schema_hash)` pairs, exactly as `StateChange`
    //!   documents, so frames are self-describing without polling.
    //! - The **router** maps `(plugin_id, method)` to a synchronous handler.
    //!   Handlers are pure value-in/value-out; async or D-Bus-backed behavior
    //!   plugs in behind `BridgeCore` call sites, not inside the router.
    //! - The **core** owns the state store and an append-only hash-chained
    //!   journal. Every accepted mutation appends one journal event and
    //!   publishes one `StateChange` frame. `VerifyChain` recomputes the
    //!   chain, so audit needs no external store.
    //! - The **service** layer is a thin tonic translation of the three
    //!   proto services onto the core. `EventChainService` proof/snapshot
    //!   RPCs are honestly `UNIMPLEMENTED`; everything else is real.
    //!
    //! - OvsdbMirror, RuntimeMirror, ComponentRegistry, MailService, PrivacyNetworkService, DbusPassthrough — dropped, surface already covered by plugin state/catalog.
    //! - HookProvider — dropped from bridge, hooks move to the EMQX plugin (user-defined category field, separate work).
    //! - RegistrationService — dropped, super old, fresh start later.
    //!
    //! Deliberately gone (the old pollution): build-time live-host schema
    //! capture, generated per-plugin protos, chat-router/tched-router legacy,
    //! and the ~140 dispatch modules. Old files remain on disk unreferenced;
    //! remove them with `git rm` when convenient — they no longer compile
    //! into this crate (see `autobins`/`autotests` in Cargo.toml).

    pub mod catalog;
    pub mod core;
    pub mod grpc_client;
    pub mod grant_document;
    pub mod human_principal_registry;
    pub mod identity_binding;
    pub mod identity_receiver;
    pub mod mqtt_doorbell_relay;
    pub mod oracle_assertion;
    #[allow(dead_code)] // Receiver is not mounted until all identity paths are wired.
    pub(crate) mod oracle_receiver;
    #[cfg(test)]
    mod oracle_test_support;
    pub mod router;
    pub mod server;
    pub mod sid1_checks;
    #[allow(dead_code)] // The reader is not mounted until request admission is wired.
    pub(crate) mod state_reader;
    pub mod tls_door;

    /// Generated protobuf types for `package operation.v1`.
    pub mod proto {
        tonic::include_proto!("operation.v1");
    
        /// Combined descriptor set for gRPC reflection.
        pub const FILE_DESCRIPTOR_SET: &[u8] =
            tonic::include_file_descriptor_set!("operation_descriptor");
    }
    
    pub use catalog::{Catalog, CatalogError, PluginEntry, PluginMethod};
    pub use core::{BridgeCore, Journal, StateStore};
    pub use grpc_client::{
        GhostbridgeCallMetadata, GrpcClientPool, RemoteEndpoint, RemoteOperationClient,

    //! Fresh bridge binary: serves `StateSync`, `PluginService` and
    //! `EventChainService` (plus reflection) via [`op_grpc_bridge::serve`].
    //!
    //! Listen address: `OP_GRPC_BRIDGE_LISTEN`, else `OP_DBUS_GRPC_LISTEN`,
    //! else `0.0.0.0:50051`. Catalog source: `OP_BRIDGE_CATALOG` (path to a
    //! catalog JSON file), else an empty catalog.
    
    use std::net::SocketAddr;
    
    use op_grpc_bridge::core::BridgeCore;
    use op_grpc_bridge::Catalog;
    
    #[tokio::main]
    async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        let _ = rustls::crypto::aws_lc_rs::default_provider().install_default();
        tracing_subscriber::fmt()
            .with_env_filter(
                tracing_subscriber::EnvFilter::try_from_default_env()
                    .unwrap_or_else(|_| tracing_subscriber::EnvFilter::new("info")),
            )
            .init();
    
        let addr: SocketAddr = std::env::var("OP_GRPC_BRIDGE_LISTEN")
            .or_else(|_| std::env::var("OP_DBUS_GRPC_LISTEN"))
            .unwrap_or_else(|_| "0.0.0.0:50051".to_string())
            .parse()?;
    
        let catalog = match std::env::var("OP_BRIDGE_CATALOG") {
            Ok(path) => Catalog::from_json_str(&std::fs::read_to_string(&path)?)?,
            Err(_) => Catalog::empty(),
        };
    
        tracing::info!(%addr, plugins = catalog.plugins().len(), "op-grpc-bridge starting");
        op_grpc_bridge::serve(addr, BridgeCore::new(catalog)).await
    }

     3 files changed, 101 insertions(+), 1965 deletions(-)
    //! D-Bus ↔ gRPC Bidirectional Bridge
    //!
    //! Provides live synchronization between D-Bus objects and gRPC services:
    //! - D-Bus property changes → gRPC streaming updates
    //! - gRPC mutations → D-Bus method calls / property sets
    //! - D-Bus signals → gRPC server-streaming
    //! - All changes flow through the event chain for audit/compliance
    //!
    //! Architecture:
    //! ```text
    //!                     ┌─────────────────┐
    //!                     │   Event Chain   │ ← Source of truth
    //!                     │  (audit + hash) │
    //!                     └────────┬────────┘
    //!                              │
    //!               ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
    //!               ▼                              ▼
    //!     ┌─────────────────┐            ┌─────────────────┐
    //!     │     D-Bus       │◄──────────►│      gRPC       │
    //!     │  (local IPC)    │            │  (remote RPC)   │
    //!     └─────────────────┘            └─────────────────┘
    //! ```

    /// SID1 verified against committed state, its binding and the active principal registry.
    #[derive(Clone)]
    pub struct VerifiedSid1(SealedId);
    
    pub(crate) struct BoundSid1(SealedId);
    
    impl BoundSid1 {
        pub(crate) fn claims(&self) -> &SealedId {
            &self.0
        }
    }
    
    impl std::fmt::Debug for VerifiedSid1 {
        fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
            formatter.write_str("VerifiedSid1([redacted])")
        }

    impl VerifiedSid1 {

            &self.0
        }

    #[derive(Deserialize)]
    struct CompiledIdentityContract {
        version: String,
        fields: HashMap<String, FieldSchema>,
    }
    
    fn pinned_identity(dir: &Path) -> anyhow::Result<crate::catalog::PluginEntry> {
        let pinned = Catalog::sealed_plugin(dir, "identity_sled")?;
        let schema: op_state_store::PluginSchema = serde_json::from_value(
            pinned
                .schema
                .clone()
                .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("sealed identity schema absent"))?,
        )?;
        let compiled: CompiledIdentityContract = serde_json::from_str(include_str!(concat!(
            env!("OUT_DIR"),
            "/identity_state_contract.json"
        )))?;
        anyhow::ensure!(
            schema.version == compiled.version && schema.fields == compiled.fields,
            "compiled and sealed identity state contracts differ"
        );
        Ok(pinned)
    }
    
    fn committed_session(
        catalog_dir: &Path,
        state_dir: &str,
        session_id: &str,
    ) -> anyhow::Result<Option<ContainerIdentitySled>> {
        let before = pinned_identity(catalog_dir)?;
        let bytes =
            op_core::projection_shm::read_credential_projection_bytes_in(state_dir, "identity_sled")?
                .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("committed identity credential projection is absent"))?;
        let after = pinned_identity(catalog_dir)?;
        anyhow::ensure!(
            before.schema_hash == after.schema_hash
                && before.sealed_schema_json == after.sealed_schema_json,
            "identity plugin seal changed during credential state access"
        );
        let value: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_slice(&bytes)?;
        anyhow::ensure!(
            value.get("sleds").is_some_and(serde_json::Value::is_array),
            "identity sleds missing"
        );
        anyhow::ensure!(
            value.get("events").is_some_and(serde_json::Value::is_array),
            "identity events missing"
        );
        let state: IdentitySledState = serde_json::from_value(value)?;
        let mut ids = HashSet::new();
        for sled in &state.sleds {
            anyhow::ensure!(
                ids.insert(sled.session_id.as_str()),
                "duplicate identity in SHM"
            );
            crate::identity_binding::validate_sled(sled)?;
        }
        let mut events = HashSet::new();
        for event in &state.events {
            anyhow::ensure!(
                events.insert((event.session_id.as_str(), event.seq)),
                "duplicate identity event in SHM"
            );
        }
        Ok(state
            .sleds
            .into_iter()
            .find(|sled| sled.session_id == session_id))
    }
    
    pub(crate) fn verify_in(
        catalog_dir: &Path,
        state_dir: &str,
        wire: &[u8],
        transport: &str,
        now: i64,
    ) -> anyhow::Result<BoundSid1> {
        let claims =
            crate::sid1_checks::parse_for_transport(wire, transport).map_err(anyhow::Error::msg)?;
        let sled = committed_session(catalog_dir, state_dir, &claims.session_id)?
            .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("sealed identity session was not found"))?;
        let claims = crate::sid1_checks::match_bound_session(wire, &sled, transport, now)
            .map_err(anyhow::Error::msg)?;
        Ok(BoundSid1(claims))
    }
    
    /// Find the authored SID1 for an already anchored assertion key. This never
    /// mints or changes an identity, and reads only the committed private projection.
    pub(crate) fn bound_session_for_key_in(
        catalog_dir: &Path,
        state_dir: &str,
        key: &str,
        now: i64,
    ) -> anyhow::Result<BoundSid1> {
        let session_id = op_identity::session::derive_session_id(key);
        let sled = committed_session(catalog_dir, state_dir, &session_id)?
            .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("assertion has no committed identity session"))?;
        let encoded = sled
            .sealed_id
            .as_deref()
            .and_then(|value| value.strip_prefix(op_identity::sealed_id::INLINE_PREFIX))
            .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("committed identity credential is unavailable"))?;
        let wire = base64::engine::general_purpose::URL_SAFE_NO_PAD.decode(encoded)?;
        let claims = crate::sid1_checks::match_bound_session(&wire, &sled, "grpc", now)
            .map_err(anyhow::Error::msg)?;
        anyhow::ensure!(
            claims.wireguard_pubkey == key,
            "assertion key does not match committed identity"
        );
        Ok(BoundSid1(claims))
    }

        anyhow::ensure!(

    pub(crate) const CONTROL_PLANE_CHATBOT_CONTAINER: &str = "3tchedChatbot";
    pub(crate) const RESERVED_CHATBOT_CONTAINER: &str = "3tchedCtlChatbot";
    
    pub fn configured_chatbot_key() -> Option<String> {
        std::env::var("OP_CONTROL_PLANE_CHATBOT_WIREGUARD_PUBKEY")
            .ok()
            .map(|value| value.trim().to_owned())
            .filter(|value| !value.is_empty())

    fn chatbot_binding_matches(
        sled: &ContainerIdentitySled,
        instance: &IncusInstance,
        configured_session: Option<&str>,
        configured_key: Option<&str>,
    ) -> bool {
        instance.name == CONTROL_PLANE_CHATBOT_CONTAINER
            && instance.instance_type == "container"
            && sled.principal_kind.as_deref() == Some("service")
            && configured_session == Some(sled.session_id.as_str())
            && configured_key == Some(sled.wireguard_pubkey.as_str())
            && op_identity::session::derive_session_id(&sled.wireguard_pubkey) == sled.session_id
            && instance.config.as_ref().is_some_and(|config| {
                config.get("user.opdbus.session_id") == Some(&sled.session_id)
                    && config.get("user.opdbus.wireguard_public_key") == Some(&sled.wireguard_pubkey)
            })
    }
    
    pub fn identity_instance_matches(sled: &ContainerIdentitySled, instance: &IncusInstance) -> bool {
        // The native name is a label. Ownership remains the stored UUID, session
        // and key binding, not the label's number or its creation receipt.
        let named = (op_cozo_store::is_numbered_native_name(&instance.name)
            || (instance.name == RESERVED_CHATBOT_CONTAINER
                && sled.principal_kind.as_deref() == Some("service")
                && control_plane_chatbot_session_id().as_deref() == Some(sled.session_id.as_str())
                && configured_chatbot_key().as_deref() == Some(sled.wireguard_pubkey.as_str())
                && op_identity::session::derive_session_id(&sled.wireguard_pubkey) == sled.session_id))
            && instance.instance_type == "container"
            && instance.config.as_ref().is_some_and(|c| {
                c.get("user.opdbus.session_id") == Some(&sled.session_id)
                    && c.get("user.opdbus.wireguard_public_key") == Some(&sled.wireguard_pubkey)
                    && c.get("volatile.uuid")
                        .is_some_and(|v| uuid::Uuid::parse_str(v).is_ok())
            })
            && sled.instance.as_ref().is_some_and(|stored| {
                stored.name == instance.name
                    && stored
                        .config
                        .as_ref()
                        .zip(instance.config.as_ref())
                        .is_some_and(|(a, b)| a.get("volatile.uuid") == b.get("volatile.uuid"))
            });
        named
            || (instance.name == sled.session_id && instance.instance_type == "container")
            || chatbot_binding_matches(
                sled,
                instance,
                control_plane_chatbot_session_id().as_deref(),
                configured_chatbot_key().as_deref(),
            )
    }
    
    pub fn identity_session_binding_matches(sled: &ContainerIdentitySled) -> bool {
        match sled.instance.as_ref() {
            Some(instance) => identity_instance_matches(sled, instance),
            // The identity owner explicitly initializes humans without per-account
            // containers. Actor class comes from the committed record, not SID1 or
            // request metadata; any attached instance must still match above.
            None => sled.principal_kind.as_deref() == Some("human"),
        }
    }
    
    pub fn validate_sled(sled: &ContainerIdentitySled) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        anyhow::ensure!(!sled.session_id.is_empty(), "identity session id is empty");
        anyhow::ensure!(
            sled.mutation_index <= i64::MAX as u64,
            "mutation index overflow"

        if let Some(instance) = &sled.instance {
            anyhow::ensure!(

                    .is_some_and(|value| !value.is_empty()),

            );
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    //! Method router: `(plugin_id, method)` -> synchronous handler.
    //!
    //! Handlers are pure value-in/value-out functions over JSON values. Async or
    //! D-Bus-backed behavior plugs in behind [`BridgeCore`](crate::core::BridgeCore)
    //! call sites, not inside the router.
    
    use std::collections::HashMap;
    use std::sync::{Arc, RwLock};
    
    /// A synchronous value-in/value-out method handler.
    #[derive(Clone)]
    pub struct Handler(
        Arc<dyn Fn(&[serde_json::Value]) -> Result<serde_json::Value, RouterError> + Send + Sync>,
    );
    
    impl Handler {
        /// Wrap a plain closure as a handler.
        pub fn new<F>(f: F) -> Self
        where
            F: Fn(&[serde_json::Value]) -> Result<serde_json::Value, RouterError>
                + Send
                + Sync
                + 'static,
        {
            Self(Arc::new(f))
        }
    
        /// Run the handler.
        pub fn call(&self, args: &[serde_json::Value]) -> Result<serde_json::Value, RouterError> {
            (self.0)(args)
        }
    }
    
    impl<F> From<F> for Handler
    where
        F: Fn(&[serde_json::Value]) -> Result<serde_json::Value, RouterError> + Send + Sync + 'static,
    {
        fn from(f: F) -> Self {
            Self::new(f)
        }
    }
    
    impl std::fmt::Debug for Handler {
        fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
            f.write_str("Handler(..)")
        }
    }
    
    /// Router failure: unknown route, or a handler that returned an error.
    #[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
    pub enum RouterError {
        /// No route table entry for this plugin at all.
        #[error("unknown plugin: {0}")]
        UnknownPlugin(String),
        /// Plugin is routed, but this method is not.
        #[error("unknown method '{method}' for plugin '{plugin_id}'")]
        UnknownMethod { plugin_id: String, method: String },
        /// The handler ran and failed.
        #[error("handler for '{plugin_id}.{method}' failed: {message}")]
        HandlerFailed {
            plugin_id: String,
            method: String,
            message: String,
        },
    }
    
    /// Synchronous `(plugin_id, method)` dispatch table. Cheap to clone.
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, Default)]
    pub struct Router {
        routes: Arc<RwLock<HashMap<String, HashMap<String, Handler>>>>,
    }
    
    impl Router {
        /// An empty router.
        pub fn new() -> Self {
            Self::default()
        }
    
        /// Register (or replace) the handler for one route.
        pub fn register(
            &self,
            plugin_id: impl Into<String>,
            method: impl Into<String>,
            handler: Handler,
        ) {
            self.routes
                .write()
                .expect("router lock poisoned")
                .entry(plugin_id.into())
                .or_default()
                .insert(method.into(), handler);
        }
    
        /// Is a handler registered for this route?
        pub fn has(&self, plugin_id: &str, method: &str) -> bool {
            self.routes
                .read()
                .expect("router lock poisoned")
                .get(plugin_id)
                .is_some_and(|methods| methods.contains_key(method))
        }
    
        /// Dispatch one call. The table lock is released before the handler runs.
        pub fn call(
            &self,
            plugin_id: &str,
            method: &str,
            args: &[serde_json::Value],
        ) -> Result<serde_json::Value, RouterError> {
            let handler = {
                let routes = self.routes.read().expect("router lock poisoned");
                let methods = routes
                    .get(plugin_id)
                    .ok_or_else(|| RouterError::UnknownPlugin(plugin_id.to_string()))?;
                methods
                    .get(method)
                    .cloned()
                    .ok_or_else(|| RouterError::UnknownMethod {
                        plugin_id: plugin_id.to_string(),
                        method: method.to_string(),
                    })?
            };
            handler.call(args).map_err(|err| match err {
                // A handler that returns routing errors is confused; normalize.
                RouterError::HandlerFailed { .. } => err,
                other => RouterError::HandlerFailed {
                    plugin_id: plugin_id.to_string(),
                    method: method.to_string(),
                    message: other.to_string(),
                },
            })
        }
    }

    pub struct NativeCreationRecord {

    pub fn is_numbered_native_name(name: &str) -> bool {

            number.parse::<i64>().is_ok_and(|n| n > 0 && n.to_string() == number)
        })
    }
    
    fn is_chatbot_reservation(request: &NativeCreationRequest) -> bool {
        request.reserved_name.as_deref() == Some("3tchedCtlChatbot")
            && request.owner_kind == "identity"

    fn records(tx: &MultiTransaction) -> std::result::Result<Vec<NativeCreationRecord>, CozoError> {
        query(tx, "?[document,operation_id] := *native_container_creations{document,operation_id}", Params::new())?
            .rows.iter().map(|row| {
                let record: NativeCreationRecord = serde_json::from_str(&string(row, 0)?)?;
                if string(row, 1)? != record.request.operation_id
                    || record.request.schema_hash.is_empty()
                    || !valid_root_repair_digest(&record.request.request_digest)
                    || (if record.request.reserved_name.is_some() {
                        !is_chatbot_reservation(&record.request)
                            || record.number != 0 || record.name != "3tchedCtlChatbot"
                    } else {
                        record.number <= 0 || record.name != format!("ID-{}", record.number)
                    })
                    || !matches!(record.phase.as_str(), "intent" | "bound" | "complete")
                    || (record.phase != "intent" && uuid::Uuid::parse_str(&record.native_uuid)
                        .map_or(true, |id| id.to_string() != record.native_uuid))
                {
                    return Err(err("native creation journal is corrupt"));
                }
                Ok(record)
            }).collect()
    }
    
    fn put(tx: &MultiTransaction, record: &NativeCreationRecord) -> std::result::Result<(), CozoError> {
        query(tx, "?[operation_id,document] <- [[$op,$doc]] :put native_container_creations {operation_id => document}",
            BTreeMap::from([
                ("op".into(), DataValue::Str(record.request.operation_id.as_str().into())),
                ("doc".into(), DataValue::Str(serde_json::to_string(record)?.into())),
            ]))?;
        Ok(())
    }
    
    fn sequence(tx: &MultiTransaction, rows: &[NativeCreationRecord])
        -> std::result::Result<(i64, String), CozoError>
    {
        let result = query(tx, "?[next,pending] := *native_container_sequence{key,next,pending}, key = 'default'", Params::new())?;
        let (next, pending) = match result.rows.as_slice() {
            [] if rows.is_empty() => {
                let marker = query(tx, "?[completed] := *schema_migrations{name,completed}, name = 'native-container-sequence-v1'", Params::new())?;
                if !marker.rows.is_empty() { return Err(err("native creation sequence is missing; refusing reset")); }
                (1, String::new())
            }
            [row] => (integer(row, 0)?, string(row, 1)?),
            _ => return Err(err("native creation sequence is missing or corrupt")),
        };
        // Container zero shares the durable POST fence but never advances ID-N.
        let special = rows.iter().filter(|r| is_chatbot_reservation(&r.request)).collect::<Vec<_>>();
        if special.len() > 1 || special.iter().any(|r| r.phase != "complete" && r.request.operation_id != pending) {
            return Err(err("reserved chatbot creation history or fence differs"));
        }
        let special_pending = special.iter().any(|r| r.phase != "complete" && r.request.operation_id == pending);
        let mut sorted = rows.iter().filter(|r| r.request.reserved_name.is_none()).collect::<Vec<_>>();
        sorted.sort_by_key(|r| r.number);
        let mut expected = 1i64;
        for row in sorted {
            if row.number != expected
                || (row.number < next && row.phase != "complete")
                || (row.number == next && (row.phase == "complete" || row.request.operation_id != pending))
                || row.number > next
            { return Err(err("native creation history is incomplete; refusing sequence recovery")); }
            expected = expected.checked_add(1).ok_or_else(|| err("native name sequence exhausted"))?;
        }
        if next < 1 || ((pending.is_empty() || special_pending) && expected != next)
            || (!pending.is_empty() && !special_pending && next.checked_add(1) != Some(expected))
        { return Err(err("native sequence and pending fence disagree")); }
        Ok((next, pending))
    }
    
    fn put_sequence(tx: &MultiTransaction, next: i64, pending: &str) -> std::result::Result<(), CozoError> {
        query(tx, "?[key,next,pending] <- [['default',$next,$pending]] :put native_container_sequence {key => next,pending}",
            BTreeMap::from([("next".into(), dv_int(next)), ("pending".into(), DataValue::Str(pending.into()))]))?;

    /// Pure request preparation; only the bridge's durable owner may submit it.
    pub fn native_creation_body(input: &CreateInstanceInput) -> Result<serde_json::Value> {
        anyhow::ensure!(input.name.is_empty(), "name is server assigned; omit name for ID-N creation");
        anyhow::ensure!(matches!(input.instance_type.as_str(), "container" | "virtual-machine"), "invalid Incus instance type");
        let source = match input.source_mode.as_str() {
            "image" => image_source(&input.image)?,
            "empty" if input.image.is_empty() => serde_json::json!({"type":"none"}),
            _ => anyhow::bail!("source_mode must be image with image, or empty without image"),
        };
        let config = input.config.clone().unwrap_or_default();
        validate_config(&config)?;
        anyhow::ensure!(!config.contains_key("user.opdbus.creation_operation")
            && !config.contains_key("user.opdbus.creation_digest"),
            "creation receipt markers are server assigned");
        let mut devices = BTreeMap::new();
        for named in &input.devices {
            validate_segment(&named.name, "device name")?;
            anyhow::ensure!(devices.insert(named.name.clone(), named.device.to_incus_map()).is_none(), "duplicate Incus device name");
        }
        Ok(serde_json::json!({"type":input.instance_type,"source":source,
            "profiles":input.profiles,"config":config,"devices":devices,"ephemeral":false}))
    }

        ensure!(raw["name"] == record.name && raw["type"] == body["type"]
            && raw["config"]["user.opdbus.creation_operation"] == record.request.operation_id
            && raw["config"]["user.opdbus.creation_digest"] == record.request.request_digest,
            "native creation ownership markers differ");
        if record.phase != "complete" {
            ensure!(raw["status"] == "Stopped" && raw["status_code"] == 102
                && raw["profiles"] == body["profiles"] && raw["devices"] == body["devices"],
                "native preparation is not the pinned stopped definition");
            if record.request.owner_kind == "identity" {
                ensure!(raw["expanded_config"]["security.privileged"] == "false"
                    && raw["expanded_config"]["security.nesting"] == "false"
                    && raw["expanded_config"]["boot.autostart"] == "false"
                    && raw["expanded_config"]["raw.lxc"] == body["config"]["raw.lxc"],
                    "expanded native identity security differs");
                let expanded = raw["expanded_devices"].as_object().context("expanded devices absent")?;

                    && expanded.get("runtime-run") == body["devices"].get("runtime-run")
                    && expanded.get("fuse") == body["devices"].get("fuse")
                    && expanded.get("lungs-socket-dir") == Some(&json!({"type":"disk", "source":"/run/opdbus/lungs",
                        "path":"/run/opdbus/lungs", "readonly":"true"})), "expanded identity devices differ");
            }
            for (key, value) in body["config"].as_object().context("creation config missing")? {
                ensure!(raw["config"].get(key) == Some(value), "native creation config differs");

    }

        /// Fresh discovery for native clients. These are the mounted declarations,
